title: What is the difference between a Load Balancer (L4 vs L7), a Reverse Proxy, and an API Gateway, and why are they complementary rather than alternatives?
shortTitle: What is the difference between a Load Balancer (L4 vs L7), a Reverse Proxy, and an API Gateway, and why are they complementary rather than alternatives?

s1_definition.profdef: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend instances to spread load and provide high availability; an L4 load balancer routes by IP and port without inspecting the payload, while an L7 load balancer inspects the HTTP request (path, headers, cookies) and can route based on content. A reverse proxy is a server that sits in front of backend servers and forwards client requests to them, adding capabilities like TLS termination, caching, compression, and request routing while hiding the backends. An API gateway is a specialized L7 reverse proxy for microservices that adds API-specific concerns: authentication, authorization, rate limiting, request aggregation, protocol translation, and per-route policies. They are complementary layers rather than alternatives because each operates at a different concern level, and a production stack often uses all three stacked together.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the entrance to National Bank of India's main branch. The load balancer is the floor manager who directs each arriving customer to whichever teller window is free, so no single teller is swamped; an L4 manager just counts heads and sends people to the shortest line without caring why they came, while an L7 manager reads the customer's form and sends loan customers to the loan desk and deposit customers to the deposit desk. The reverse proxy is the front reception that greets everyone, checks their umbrella (TLS), hands out pre-printed answers to common questions (caching), and shields the staff behind so customers never see the back office directly. The API gateway is the specialized security-and-service desk for a modern branch full of specialist departments: it checks your ID (authentication), confirms you are allowed at that department (authorization), limits how often you can ask (rate limiting), and can collect answers from several departments into one reply (aggregation). The bank uses all three together, not one instead of another.
s1_definition.oneliner: A load balancer spreads traffic across instances, a reverse proxy fronts and shields backends with TLS and caching, and an API gateway adds API-specific auth, rate limiting, and aggregation — they stack as complementary layers, not competing choices.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend instances to spread load and provide high availability; an L4 load balancer routes by IP and port without inspecting the payload, while an L7 load balancer inspects the HTTP request (path, headers, cookies) and can route based on content. A reverse proxy is a server that sits in front of backend servers and forwards client requests to them, adding capabilities like TLS termination, caching, compression, and request routing while hiding the backends. An API gateway is a specialized L7 reverse proxy for microservices that adds API-specific concerns: authentication, authorization, rate limiting, request aggregation, protocol translation, and per-route policies. They are complementary layers rather than alternatives because each operates at a different concern level, and a production stack often uses all three stacked together.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the entrance to National Bank of India's main branch. The load balancer is the floor manager who directs each arriving customer to whichever teller window is free, so no single teller is swamped; an L4 manager just counts heads and sends people to the shortest line without caring why they came, while an L7 manager reads the customer's form and sends loan customers to the loan desk and deposit customers to the deposit desk. The reverse proxy is the front reception that greets everyone, checks their umbrella (TLS), hands out pre-printed answers to common questions (caching), and shields the staff behind so customers never see the back office directly. The API gateway is the specialized security-and-service desk for a modern branch full of specialist departments: it checks your ID (authentication), confirms you are allowed at that department (authorization), limits how often you can ask (rate limiting), and can collect answers from several departments into one reply (aggregation). The bank uses all three together, not one instead of another.

**One line to remember:** A load balancer spreads traffic across instances, a reverse proxy fronts and shields backends with TLS and caching, and an API gateway adds API-specific auth, rate limiting, and aggregation — they stack as complementary layers, not competing choices.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the load balancer because its job is the narrowest: take incoming connections and distribute them across a pool of backend instances so that load is spread and the system stays available if an instance dies. The crucial distinction is the OSI layer at which it works. An L4 (transport layer) load balancer routes based on IP address and TCP/UDP port only; it does not look inside the packet, so it is extremely fast and protocol-agnostic, but it cannot make decisions based on the HTTP path or headers. An L7 (application layer) load balancer terminates the connection and inspects the HTTP request, so it can route `/loans` to the loan service and `/payments` to the payment service, do sticky sessions by cookie, and retry failed requests, at the cost of more processing per request. A small configuration example of L7 routing is a rule that says requests whose path starts with `/api/loans` go to the loan backend pool and requests to `/api/payments` go to the payment pool.

A reverse proxy sits in front of one or more backend servers and forwards client requests to them, returning the backends' responses to the client. The client thinks it is talking to the proxy; the real servers are hidden behind it. Beyond forwarding, a reverse proxy commonly does TLS termination (it holds the certificate and decrypts HTTPS so backends can speak plain HTTP), caching of responses, compression, serving static content, and basic path-based routing. Nginx and HAProxy are classic reverse proxies. Note the overlap: an L7 load balancer is essentially a reverse proxy that emphasizes distribution, and a reverse proxy often also load-balances, so the categories blur, which is exactly why people confuse them.

An API gateway is a specialized L7 reverse proxy built for microservices, and it adds concerns that are specific to serving APIs to clients. These include authentication (validating a JWT or API key), authorization (checking the caller may access this route), rate limiting and quotas (so one client cannot overwhelm the system), request routing to the right microservice, request and response transformation and protocol translation (for example REST on the outside, gRPC to the services), request aggregation (calling several services and combining the result so a mobile client makes one call instead of five), and per-route policies, metrics, and tracing. Kong, Spring Cloud Gateway, AWS API Gateway, and Apigee are examples. A small conceptual example: a gateway route says "for POST /api/v1/transfers, require a valid JWT with scope transfers:write, apply a limit of 100 requests per minute per client, then forward to the transfer-service".

Why are they complementary rather than alternatives? Because each addresses a different concern level and they stack naturally. A typical production stack looks like this from outside in: DNS resolves to an external L4 load balancer spreading raw traffic across availability zones; behind it an L7 reverse proxy or ingress terminates TLS and does path routing; behind that an API gateway enforces authentication, rate limiting, and aggregation; and the gateway forwards to microservices, which may themselves sit behind an internal load balancer for their instances. You do not pick one of these; you compose them, each doing what it does best. A senior nuance is to keep business logic out of the gateway — the gateway handles cross-cutting concerns, not domain rules, because a "god gateway" stuffed with business logic becomes a deployment bottleneck and a single point of coupling. Another nuance is that L4 is preferred at the very edge for raw throughput and DDoS absorption, while L7 intelligence belongs closer to the services.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India exposes microservices (loans, payments, accounts) to mobile and web clients and must route, secure, and scale traffic.

Problem 1 — One service is overwhelmed. At peak, all traffic hit a single instance of the payment service and it fell over while other instances sat idle. This is the load-balancer problem: traffic must be spread across instances, and an L4 balancer at the edge plus an L7 balancer per service solves it.

Problem 2 — Backends exposed and unprotected. Clients connected straight to services over plain HTTP, certificates were duplicated everywhere, and there was no single place to enforce authentication or rate limits. This needs a reverse proxy for TLS termination and shielding, and an API gateway for auth, rate limiting, and aggregation.

The fix is a layered edge: an L4 load balancer spreads raw connections, an L7 reverse proxy terminates TLS and routes by path, and an API gateway authenticates, rate-limits, and routes to the right service. We will model the request passing through all three layers in order.

The code will have a `LoadBalancerL4` that picks a backend by connection count, a `ReverseProxy` that terminates TLS and routes by path, an `ApiGateway` that authenticates, rate-limits, and forwards, and a `BackendService` representing a microservice instance. The demo sends requests through the full stack, shows each layer's responsibility, and shows a request rejected by rate limiting and one rejected by authentication.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001) sends four authenticated requests to /api/loans with a rate limit of three per minute, then Priya (CUR3001) sends one unauthenticated request.

Step 1 — The first request reaches the API gateway. The gateway authenticates it (valid JWT), checks the rate limit (first of three, allowed), and forwards it down. The gateway handled API-specific concerns only.

Step 2 — The reverse proxy receives the forwarded request. It terminates TLS (so the backend speaks plain HTTP) and routes by path /api/loans to the loan pool, then hands down to the L4 load balancer. The proxy shielded the backends and handled transport concerns.

Step 3 — The L4 load balancer picks the loan backend with the fewest connections without inspecting the HTTP payload, increments its connection count, and forwards. This is pure distribution.

Step 4 — The backend instance serves the loan data and returns 200. The response travels back up through the same layers to the client.

Step 5 — The second and third requests follow the same path. The fourth request is authenticated but exceeds the three-per-minute limit, so the gateway rejects it with 429 before it ever reaches the proxy, backend, or load balancer — the gateway protected the backends.

Step 6 — Priya's request is unauthenticated, so the gateway rejects it with 401 immediately. Authentication is the gateway's job, not the load balancer's, which is why these layers are complementary — each stops a different kind of bad request at the right level.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A load balancer, a reverse proxy, and an API gateway are often confused because their jobs overlap, but they operate at different concern levels and in practice you stack all three. A load balancer's narrow job is to distribute incoming traffic across multiple backend instances for load spreading and availability. The key distinction is the layer: an L4 load balancer routes purely by IP and port without looking inside the packet, so it is extremely fast and protocol-agnostic but cannot route by HTTP path, whereas an L7 load balancer terminates the connection and inspects the HTTP request so it can route by path, header, or cookie at the cost of more work per request.

A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers and forwards client requests to them, hiding the backends so the client only ever talks to the proxy. On top of forwarding it commonly does TLS termination so it holds the certificate and backends speak plain HTTP, plus caching, compression, and basic path routing. The overlap is real: an L7 load balancer is essentially a reverse proxy that emphasizes distribution, which is exactly why people mix them up.

An API gateway is a specialized L7 reverse proxy built for microservices, adding API-specific concerns: authenticating a JWT or API key, authorizing the route, rate limiting so one client cannot overwhelm the system, routing to the right service, protocol translation such as REST outside and gRPC inside, and request aggregation so a mobile client makes one call instead of five. In my banking edge, the gateway rejected unauthenticated requests with 401 and rate-limited abusive clients with 429 before they ever reached the backends.

The reason they are complementary rather than alternatives is that each stops a different kind of problem at the right level, and a real stack composes them from outside in: an L4 load balancer at the edge spreads raw traffic and absorbs floods, an L7 reverse proxy terminates TLS and routes by path, an API gateway enforces authentication, rate limiting, and aggregation, and the services themselves sit behind internal load balancers. You do not choose one; you layer them. The senior point I always add is to keep business logic out of the gateway, because a god gateway stuffed with domain rules becomes a deployment bottleneck and a coupling point.

The one-line summary I give is that a load balancer spreads traffic across instances, a reverse proxy fronts and shields backends with TLS and caching, and an API gateway adds API-level auth, rate limiting, and aggregation, and because each handles a different concern they stack together as layers rather than competing as alternatives.
